displayQuote: How do I love thee? Let me count the ways

meta.title: Who really said "How do I love thee? Let me count the ways"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote it. It's the exact opening line of Sonnet 43 of Sonnets from the Portuguese, published 1850.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Elizabeth Barrett Browning: the verbatim first line of Sonnet 43 of Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850). Often mis-credited to Shakespeare.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the verbatim opening line of Sonnet 43 (“XLIII”) of Sonnets from the Portuguese, the 44-sonnet love sequence Browning first published in 1850. The wording is exact and the source is firmly documented.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Petrarchan sonnet; 14 lines of iambic pentameter

source.excerpt:
How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.
I love thee to the depth and breadth and height
My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight
For the ends of being and ideal grace.
trail: The Poetry Foundation prints the sonnet with this exact opening line.
The Academy of American Poets reproduces the same line verbatim and flags the text as public domain.
Wikipedia records that the 44-sonnet sequence was first published in 1850 and calls this line “one of the most famous in English poetry.”
source.excerptNote: The opening quatrain of Sonnet 43; the question of the first line is answered across the remaining thirteen.

author.name: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
author.heading: About Elizabeth Barrett Browning
author.bio: Elizabeth Barrett Browning was one of the most celebrated English poets of the Victorian era, admired in her lifetime on both sides of the Atlantic. The 44 sonnets of Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850) trace the private courtship that led to her marriage to fellow poet Robert Browning; she framed the deeply personal sequence as if it were translated verse to soften its intimacy. Sonnet 43 became her most quoted work and one of the best-loved love poems in the language.

misattribution.heading: The mix-up
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Elizabeth Barrett Browning is correct. The common error is confusing who wrote it — the archaic “thee” and the sonnet form lead many to assume it is Shakespeare.

items.why: Because the line is a sonnet opening full of “thee,” it is often loosely credited to Shakespeare. It is not his: it is Sonnet 43 of Browning's Sonnets from the Portuguese, written some two and a half centuries after Shakespeare's sonnets.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Elizabeth Barrett Browning's, from Sonnet 43 of Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850).

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Sonnet 43 opens with a question and spends its remaining thirteen lines answering it, cataloguing the “ways” of love from everyday need to religious devotion and beyond death. That structure — a plain question met by an overflowing answer — is much of why the line is quoted at weddings and on Valentine cards to this day.

Browning wrote the sequence during her courtship with Robert Browning and, reluctant to expose something so personal, presented the poems as though translated from Portuguese. The disguise gave the collection its title and a measure of privacy for verse that was, in fact, entirely her own.
